lines.cap: **Narrator:** This is Kavya. She is twelve. Today, her family is moving out of the flat she grew up in.
**Kavya:** We have forty-seven boxes. Forty-six of them say 'MISC'. My dad did the labels.
**Narrator:** But this documentary isn't about Kavya. It's about the invisible crew that does the real moving.
**Narrator:** Whenever anything here moves, stops or turns, they did it. This is the foreman.
**Rex:** Rex. I'm the **resultant force**. Basically, the manager.
**Rex:** Everybody pushes, everybody pulls. I add it all up. Whatever's left over... is me.
**Rex:** I decide what actually happens. Speed up, slow down, turn... or nothing.
**Rex:** Nothing is my favourite.
**Rex:** Been in this business since the Big Bang. Never once been thanked.
**Rex:** People say, 'the sofa moved'. The sofa didn't move. We moved the sofa.
**Narrator:** Push and Pull. Episode thirteen: Moving Day.
**Narrator:** Seven a.m. Before the humans wake up, Rex holds the briefing.
**Rex:** Rule one. Each of us is a **push** or a **pull**. That's all a **force** is.
**Rex:** Rule two. Nobody sees us. Only what we **do**.
**Rex:** We make things **start** moving, **speed up**, **slow down**, change **direction**, or change **shape**.
**Pushpa:** Hi hi! Pushpa! I'm a **push**! It's my first day! I've been practising on a door!
**Rex:** Pushpa's an applied force. She's new. She has a lot of energy. Not literally. Different episode.
**Rex:** We're measured in **newtons**, **N**. A small apple weighs about **1 N**.
**Rex:** On paper, we're **arrows**. The arrow points the way we act. Longer arrow, bigger force.
**Narrator:** Most of the crew are **contact forces**: they only work when things touch.
**Frieda:** Frieda. **Friction**. Whatever you're doing, I'm against it.
**Norm:** Norm. **Normal force**. I push back from surfaces, at right angles. Nobody's heard of me.
**Tess:** Tess! **Tension**! I pull, in ropes and springs. I'm very, very tense.
**Narrator:** Others act from a distance, without touching. **Non-contact forces**.
**Graham:** Hello! Graham! **Gravity**! My pull on you is your **weight**. I work remotely.
**Graham:** So do my cousins, **magnetic** and **electrostatic** forces. Never touch anybody.
**Rex:** Graham pulls everything down, towards the centre of the Earth. He's very clingy.
**Narrator:** **Upthrust**, the upward push of water, has the day off. No swimming pool in this episode.
**Narrator:** Nine a.m. Kavya tries to push the sofa to the door.
**Pushpa:** Pushing! A hundred newtons! Go, go, go!
**Frieda:** A hundred newtons, straight back at you. Objection.
**Kavya:** Why is it not moving? I am pushing SO hard.
**Rex:** Because the forces are **balanced**. Same size, opposite directions. They cancel out.
**Rex:** Resultant force: **zero**. So a still sofa **stays still**. And I'm on my break.
**Norm:** Same with me. Graham pulls the sofa down, I push up just as hard. So it doesn't sink into the floor.
**Norm:** Nobody ever says thank you to the floor.
**Narrator:** Then Kavya's dad joins in.
**Pushpa:** Two of us now! Three hundred newtons!
**Frieda:** Two hundred is the most I can do. Fine. I still object.
**Rex:** Three hundred forwards, two hundred back. **Subtract**: **100 N forwards**. That's me. I'm up.
**Narrator:** **Unbalanced forces** leave a **resultant force**, which **changes the motion**. The sofa **speeds up**.
**Narrator:** In the corridor, the sofa rolls along on a trolley at a steady speed.
**Pushpa:** To keep it moving, I have to push harder and harder, right? RIGHT?
**Rex:** No.
**Rex:** Your push just equals the friction on the wheels. Balanced. So: **steady speed**, **straight line**.
**Rex:** You only need a resultant force to **change** the motion.
**Narrator:** Ten a.m. Box thirty-one. It says 'MISC'. It is very heavy.
**Kavya:** This box weighs twenty kilograms. Minimum.
**Rex:** That's its **mass**, Kavya. Not its weight.
**Rex:** **Mass** is the **amount of matter**, in **kilograms**. It never changes, wherever you take it.
**Graham:** And **weight** is me! The **force** of gravity on that mass. So it's in **newtons**!
**Graham:** **Weight = mass × gravitational field strength**. **W = m × g**!
**Graham:** On Earth, g is about **10 N/kg**. So, twenty kilograms times ten...
**Kavya:** **200 N**. That explains my arms.
**Kavya:** Can we just move to the Moon instead?
**Graham:** On the Moon, g is only **1.6 N/kg**. Same mass, but it weighs just **32 N**.
**Graham:** Please don't move to the Moon. I'd only be one sixth as attached to you.
**Narrator:** Rex checks with a **newtonmeter**: a spring balance. Inside it is Tess.
**Tess:** Pull me, I stretch! The stretch is my **extension**: new length, minus original length.
**Tess:** My extension is **proportional** to the force. Double the force, double the stretch! **Hooke's law**.
**Rex:** So a graph of force against extension is a **straight line** through the origin.
**Tess:** But only up to my **elastic limit**! Past that, I'm **permanently stretched**. I don't go back.
**Tess:** It happened to my uncle. He worked in a trampoline. He's never been the same shape.
**Narrator:** Eleven a.m. Mum has mopped the floor. Kavya is wearing socks.
**Kavya:** No, no, no, no, NO!
**Frieda:** Wet floor, smooth socks. Hardly any of me. That's why you're sliding.
**Frieda:** People think I'm the villain. Yes, I always act **against the motion**. But without me, you couldn't even **walk**.
**Frieda:** Tyres wouldn't **grip**. **Brakes** wouldn't work. You'd all slide into walls.
**Narrator:** Friction comes from tiny bumps. Even smooth surfaces are rough close up, and the bumps catch.
**Narrator:** But in the trolley's wheels, friction **wastes energy as heat**, and wears the parts out.
**Rex:** So we **reduce** it: **oil** the wheels. A **lubricant**.
**Frieda:** Objection, Rex.
**Rex:** Objection overruled.
**Narrator:** To **increase** friction, use rougher surfaces, like rubber soles. Kavya changes her shoes.
**Frieda:** Outside, in the air, I go by another name. **Air resistance**. Or **drag**.
**Frieda:** Drag is friction from air or water. The **faster** you go, the **more** of me there is.
**Rex:** That's why fast things are **streamlined**: smooth and pointed, so the air slips past.
**Frieda:** The removal lorry is not streamlined. The removal lorry is a box.
**Narrator:** Noon. The movers arrive. Their lorry takes everything **15 km** to the new flat, in **half an hour**.
**Rex:** How fast? **Speed = distance ÷ time**.
**Rex:** In metres and seconds, that's **metres per second**, **m/s**. On roads, **kilometres per hour**.
**Kavya:** Fifteen divided by a half... **30 km/h**. My grandma drives faster than that.
**Rex:** That's the **average speed**: **total distance ÷ total time**. It wasn't steady.
**Narrator:** Here's the journey as a **distance-time graph**. Time along the bottom, distance up the side.
**Rex:** A straight sloping line means a **steady speed**. And the **steeper** the line, the **faster** it's going.
**Pushpa:** That steep bit is the expressway! Wheee!
**Pushpa:** Oh no. Now the line's flat. Did we go backwards?
**Rex:** Flat means **stationary**. The distance isn't changing. That was the traffic jam.
**Rex:** Ten minutes. Not moving at all.
**Frieda:** Best ten minutes of my day.
**Narrator:** In fact, the **gradient** of a distance-time graph, its steepness, **equals the speed**.
**Narrator:** One p.m. The new flat. It smells of fresh paint.
**Narrator:** The front door is heavy. Pushpa pushes it right next to the hinges.
**Pushpa:** It's... not... turning!
**Rex:** Turning effect, Pushpa. It's called a **moment**. **Moment = force × distance from the pivot**.
**Rex:** That's the pivot. Piv. Everything turns around Piv. Piv doesn't talk.
**Rex:** Push at the handle, far from the pivot. Same force, more distance, bigger moment. Same reason long spanners work.
**Pushpa:** It opened! I didn't even push harder!
**Rex:** A seesaw **balances** when the moments are equal: **force × distance** is the same on each side.
**Narrator:** Kavya, **400 N**, one metre from Piv. Her brother, **200 N**, two metres out. **400 N m** each. Balanced.
**Kavya:** Did you just say my weight on television?
**Narrator:** Then the sofa goes down, on four tiny legs, onto the new floor.
**Norm:** Ouch. Ouch, ouch, ouch. Those legs are tiny.
**Rex:** **Pressure = force ÷ area**. Same weight on a tiny area: huge pressure. That dents floors.
**Rex:** Pressure is in **newtons per square metre**, **N/m²**. Also called **pascals**, **Pa**.
**Narrator:** Mum sticks wide felt pads under the legs. Bigger area, smaller pressure.
**Norm:** Oh. That's lovely. Nobody's ever done anything nice for me before.
**Narrator:** A sharp box cutter works the other way: tiny edge, huge pressure. It slices through tape.

chapters.title: The crew saves you some marks

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Before the credits, the crew would like to save you some marks.
**Graham:** One! **Mass** is in **kilograms**. **Weight** is a force, so it's in **newtons**!
**Pushpa:** Two! Moving things don't need a forward force to keep going. Balanced forces mean a **steady speed**!
**Frieda:** Three. Friction and drag always **oppose** the motion. And drag **grows** with speed.
**Rex:** Four. Speed is distance **divided by** time. Pressure is force **divided by** area. Don't multiply!
**Tess:** Five! Hooke's law only works up to the **elastic limit**! Ask my uncle!
**Norm:** Six. A flat line on a distance-time graph means **stationary**. Not backwards. Like me. Forever.
**Narrator:** Push and Pull will return.
**Rex:** Piv. Anything you'd like to add?
**Piv:** ...Everything revolves around me.
**Norm:** ...He's not wrong.
**Rex:** Don't encourage him.
